subject: maths
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: On the probability scale, all probabilities lie between which two values?
options: 0 and 1
-1 and 1
0 and 100
1 and 10
questions.explain: Every probability is a number from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain) inclusive.

questions.q: What is the probability of an event that is certain to happen?
questions.explain: An event that is certain to occur has a probability of exactly 1.

questions.q: What is the probability of an impossible event?
questions.explain: An event that cannot happen has a probability of 0.

questions.q: If the probability that it rains tomorrow is 0.3, what is the probability that it does not rain?
questions.explain: The probability of an event not happening is 1 minus the probability it happens: 1 - 0.3 = 0.7.

questions.q: For equally likely outcomes, the theoretical probability of an event is calculated as:
options: Number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of outcomes
Total number of outcomes ÷ number of favourable outcomes
Number of favourable outcomes × total number of outcomes
Number of favourable outcomes ÷ number of trials
questions.explain: Theoretical probability is the number of favourable outcomes divided by the total number of equally likely outcomes.

questions.q: A fair six-sided die is rolled once. What is the probability of getting an even number?
questions.explain: There are three even numbers (2, 4, 6) out of six outcomes, giving 3/6 = 1/2.

questions.q: For any experiment, the sum of the probabilities of all possible outcomes must equal:
options: The number of outcomes
questions.explain: The probabilities of all mutually exclusive outcomes of an experiment always add up to 1.

questions.q: The relative frequency of an event is found by:
options: Frequency of the event ÷ total number of trials
Total number of trials ÷ frequency of the event
Frequency of the event × total number of trials
Frequency of the event ÷ number of favourable outcomes
questions.explain: Relative frequency (experimental probability) is the number of times an event occurs divided by the total number of trials.

questions.q: As the number of trials in an experiment increases, the relative frequency of an event tends to get closer to:
options: The theoretical probability
Zero
One
The number of trials
questions.explain: With more trials the relative frequency approaches the theoretical probability of the event.

questions.q: The probability that a spinner lands on red is 0.2. In 200 spins, how many times is it expected to land on red?
questions.explain: Expected frequency = probability × number of trials = 0.2 × 200 = 40.

questions.q: The expected frequency of an event over a number of trials is calculated by:
options: Probability of the event × number of trials
Probability of the event ÷ number of trials
Number of trials ÷ probability of the event
Probability of the event + number of trials
questions.explain: Expected frequency is the probability of the event multiplied by the number of trials.

questions.q: A coin is flipped 80 times and lands on heads 36 times. What is the relative frequency of heads?
questions.explain: Relative frequency = 36 ÷ 80 = 0.45.

questions.q: For two mutually exclusive events A and B, P(A or B) is equal to:
options: P(A) + P(B)
P(A) × P(B)
P(A) - P(B)
P(A) ÷ P(B)
questions.explain: For mutually exclusive events the probability of A or B is the sum of their individual probabilities.

questions.q: For two independent events A and B, P(A and B) is equal to:
options: P(A) × P(B)
P(A) + P(B)
P(A) - P(B)
P(A) ÷ P(B)
questions.explain: For independent events the probability of both occurring is the product of their probabilities.

questions.q: Two events are described as mutually exclusive. This means that:
options: They cannot both happen at the same time
They must both happen together
One event affects the other
They always have equal probabilities
questions.explain: Mutually exclusive events have no outcomes in common, so they cannot occur simultaneously.

questions.q: Events A and B are independent with P(A) = 0.5 and P(B) = 0.4. What is P(A and B)?
questions.explain: For independent events, P(A and B) = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2.

questions.q: On a tree diagram, to find the probability of a particular sequence of outcomes you should:
options: Multiply the probabilities along the branches
Add the probabilities along the branches
Subtract the probabilities along the branches
Divide the probabilities along the branches
questions.explain: Probabilities are multiplied along the branches of a path to give the probability of that combined outcome.

questions.q: The notation P(A | B) represents:
options: The probability of A given that B has happened
The probability of A and B
The probability of A or B
The probability of neither A nor B
questions.explain: Conditional probability P(A | B) is the probability of event A occurring given that event B has already occurred.

questions.q: When two objects are drawn from a bag without replacement, the probability for the second draw:
options: Changes because the total number of objects has decreased
Stays exactly the same as the first draw
Always becomes zero
Is always 1
questions.explain: Without replacement the second event is dependent, as the total and remaining favourable objects change.

questions.q: A bag contains 3 red and 2 blue counters. Two counters are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that both are red?
questions.explain: P(both red) = 3/5 × 2/4 = 6/20 = 3/10, since the second draw is conditional on the first.
